description.summary: A winged, ape-like cryptid said to inhabit the area around Mount St. Helens and adjacent forests of western Washington. Best known from a 1994 sighting by Brian Canfield in Pierce County.
description.full: Batsquatch is a modern American cryptid associated with the volcanic and forested terrain around Mount St. Helens in Washington State. The name is a portmanteau of 'bat' and 'Sasquatch'. The creature is described as roughly nine feet tall with a humanoid, ape-like body, leathery bat-like wings, blue or purple fur, sharp teeth, yellow eyes, and a wolf- or dog-like muzzle. The most cited encounter is the April 1994 report by 18-year-old Brian Canfield, who said his pickup truck stalled on a remote road south of Mount Rainier and a winged figure landed in front of him before flying away; the Tacoma News Tribune ran the story and reporter C. R. Roberts is credited with coining the name 'Batsquatch'. Older popular accounts also tie the cryptid to the period following the 1980 eruption of Mount St. Helens, but contemporary 1980 reports are not well documented in mainstream sources.

etymology.origin: Coined in print in 1994 by Tacoma News Tribune reporter C. R. Roberts following Brian Canfield's reported encounter, blending 'bat' with 'Sasquatch'.
etymology.meaning: Portmanteau describing a Sasquatch-like being with bat wings.
etymology.first_use: 1994, in C. R. Roberts's reporting in the Tacoma News Tribune (Washington)

features.description: Large membranous wings, often described as spanning roughly 10–15 m (sometimes exaggerated to 50 ft)
Bright yellow or red glowing eyes
An elongated, canid-like snout with sharp teeth
Distinctive blue or violet fur covering the humanoid body
Talon-like or bird-like feet, in contrast to the humanoid body

physical.morphology: An apelike or humanoid body equipped with leathery bat wings and a canid-like head. There is no consistent technical description; the creature exists primarily in eyewitness narrative and pop-culture iconography.

abilities.description: Capable of flight using its membranous wings
Reported to cause vehicles to stall in its presence (Canfield account)

patterns: Reports cluster in the Mount St. Helens / Mount Rainier corridor
Encounters typically brief, on remote roads at night or twilight
Often associated with vehicle electrical anomalies

range.description: Reports center on the southern Cascades of Washington State, particularly around Mount St. Helens and Mount Rainier in Pierce, Skamania, and Lewis counties.

hotspots.name: Mount St. Helens

location.description: Stratovolcano in the southern Washington Cascades

hotspots.notes: Often cited in popular accounts as the focal point for early Batsquatch lore, post-1980 eruption

hotspots.name: Camp One Road / Lake Kapowsin area

location.description: Remote forested area south of Mount Rainier in Pierce County, Washington

hotspots.notes: Site of Brian Canfield's reported 1994 encounter

first_recorded.source: Popular accounts attribute initial sightings to the period following the 1980 Mount St. Helens eruption

peak_activity_periods.description: Brian Canfield's reported encounter and the coining of the term 'Batsquatch'
Sporadic reports and online resurgence in cryptid media

origins.cultural_roots: A modern American cryptid with no clear pre-1980s antecedents in Pacific Northwest Indigenous tradition; emerged in late 20th-century newspaper and word-of-mouth reporting around Mount St. Helens.
origins.earliest_accounts: Popular accounts cite reports following the May 18, 1980 eruption of Mount St. Helens; the first widely documented case is Brian Canfield's April 1994 encounter, reported in the Tacoma News Tribune.
origins.folklore_connections: Thematically linked to the broader 20th-century 'winged humanoid' cryptid genre, alongside Mothman and the Jersey Devil.

timeline.event: Eruption of Mount St. Helens; popular accounts associate the early Batsquatch lore with the eruption's aftermath
timeline.significance: Provides the geographic and folkloric backdrop

timeline.event: Brian Canfield reports a winged creature near Camp One Road, Pierce County, Washington; his pickup truck stalls before the encounter
timeline.significance: Foundational documented sighting; coining of the term 'Batsquatch'
timeline.source: Tacoma News Tribune (C. R. Roberts), April 1994

timeline.event: Reporter C. R. Roberts coins the name 'Batsquatch' in the Tacoma News Tribune
timeline.significance: Anchors the cryptid's name in print

history.modern_era: Batsquatch remains a regional cryptid known mainly through tabloid retellings, cryptid podcasts, and tourism marketing in Washington State. There is no scientific investigation, and reports are sparse compared to Bigfoot in the same region. A craft-beer brand sharing the name has further cemented the cryptid in regional pop culture.

notable.name: Brian Canfield encounter

location.description: Remote forest road south of Mount Rainier, Pierce County

credibility_factors: Immediate report to family and local press
Consistent retelling over the following decades

notable.description: Driving home alone at night through wooded country in Pierce County, Brian Canfield's pickup truck reportedly stalled on a remote road. He described a roughly nine-foot tall winged creature with blue fur, a wolf-like muzzle, sharp teeth, yellow eyes, and large leathery wings landing in front of his vehicle. After several minutes the creature took off and flew away; the truck then started normally. Canfield drove home and reported the incident; the story was carried by the Tacoma News Tribune, where reporter C. R. Roberts coined the name 'Batsquatch'.

factors: Coverage primarily in regional newspaper and cryptid press
credibility.notes: The defining and most widely reported Batsquatch encounter.

sources: Tacoma News Tribune (C. R. Roberts), April 1994

documentary.name: Tacoma News Tribune coverage of the Canfield encounter
documentary.description: Local newspaper article by reporter C. R. Roberts describing Brian Canfield's encounter and coining the term 'Batsquatch'.
documentary.analysis: The primary source for the modern Batsquatch legend. No corroborating physical evidence accompanied the report.

paranormal.name: Volcanic / interdimensional cryptid
paranormal.description: Batsquatch belongs to the broader winged-humanoid cryptid type associated with major geological or industrial sites; some cryptid writers tie its emergence to the energy of the Mount St. Helens eruption.
evidence_cited: Geographic association with Mount St. Helens
Reported vehicle interference echoing Mothman accounts

skeptical.name: Misidentification
skeptical.description: The Canfield report and similar accounts may reflect misidentification of large birds (great horned owls, golden eagles) at night, possibly compounded by fatigue and the influence of pop-culture cryptid imagery.
proponents: Skeptical writers on Pacific Northwest cryptids
evidence_cited: Known large nocturnal raptors in the region
Cultural priming via Mothman and Bigfoot

skeptical.name: Folkloric construct
skeptical.description: Batsquatch is best understood as a regional modern legend reinforced by media and tourism, not as a biological candidate.
evidence_cited: Heavy presence in pop culture relative to actual sighting record

stories: Post-1980 Mount St. Helens flying-creature stories
folklore.beliefs: Treated locally as a quirky regional cryptid, often invoked in tourism, brewery branding, and cryptid media.

literature: Loren Coleman & Jerome Clark, Cryptozoology A to Z (1999) — entry for Batsquatch
other: Rogue Ales Batsquatch Hazy IPA (Oregon brewery branding)
Local Mount St. Helens / Mount Rainier tourism material

research.ongoing_studies: No active scientific investigation. The phenomenon is documented primarily in cryptid media and local press archives.
